# Vault 112
Vault 112 is a fictional underground fallout shelter (a Vault) in the Fallout video game series, notably featured in the main quest of Fallout 3 (2008). It is located in the Capital Wasteland (the post-apocalyptic Washington, D.C. area) and concealed beneath an old garage west of Evergreen Mills. Vault 112 is the site of the infamous “Tranquility Lane” simulation, a virtual reality experiment overseen by Vault 112’s creator and overseer, Dr. Stanislaus Braun. In the game’s storyline set in 2277, the player’s character (the Lone Wanderer) ventures into Vault 112 while searching for their missing father, James, only to find him and the vault’s inhabitants trapped in an idyllic 1950s-style VR world controlled by Braun.
## Design and Purpose
In the lore of Fallout, Vault 112 was one of the last Vault-Tec facilities constructed before the Great War. Built between 2068 and 2074, it was engineered to accommodate just 85 occupants who would live indefinitely in an immersive virtual reality environment as part of a secret social experiment. The vault’s overseer, Dr. Stanislaus Braun (a noted Vault-Tec scientist and inventor of the Garden of Eden Creation Kit), had Vault 112 designed to serve essentially as his personal research project and refuge. Within the facility, Braun installed an advanced VR simulation system using “Tranquility Lounger” pods, initially loaded with various utopian program scenarios – the last of which was Tranquility Lane, a program presenting an American suburban neighborhood frozen in the 1950s.
Once the inhabitants entered the Tranquility Lounger pods, they became immersed in the virtual world and had no means of exiting on their own. Unbeknownst to the residents, Braun retained absolute control over the simulation and their fates. He wielded this power to manipulate and torment the vault dwellers for his own amusement – even “killing” their virtual personas in horrific ways and then resetting their memories so the cycle could continue endlessly. The subjects believed they were living normal lives in an idyllic community, while in reality their bodies lay in stasis and their minds were trapped in Braun’s artificial reality. Because the human occupants were permanently incapacitated in the VR pods, Vault 112 was maintained entirely by robotic caretakers (specifically Robobrain robots) and powered by self-sufficient geothermal energy, allowing it to remain intact and functional for over two centuries without human maintenance. Vault 112 was sealed in 2075 – even before the nuclear bombs fell in 2077 – meaning Braun commenced his experiment shortly before the Great War erupted. By the time Fallout 3 takes place (2277), Vault 112 is one of the few Vaults in the region found in pristine condition, unaffected by radiation or external damage.
## Role in Fallout 3
In Fallout 3, Vault 112 plays a central role during the main storyline quest “Tranquility Lane.” The player’s character eventually tracks their father James to the hidden Vault 112 facility, entering it 200 years after it was supposed to have been occupied. Upon arrival, the vault’s robotic attendants provide the Lone Wanderer with a Vault 112 jumpsuit and instruct them to sit in an open Tranquility Lounger, which plugs them into Braun’s virtual simulation. The player then finds themselves in Tranquility Lane, presented as a black-and-white, idyllic suburban neighborhood cul-de-sac. The scenario evokes mid-20th-century American nostalgia – a “white picket fence” community where there was no war – and has been compared to an episode of The Twilight Zone for its eerie, frozen-in-time normalcy masking a darker secret.
Inside the simulation, the residents of Tranquility Lane appear as ordinary families unaware of their true situation, living out what they think are normal lives. One character, however, stands out: a little girl named “Betty”, who is actually Dr. Stanislaus Braun in disguise. Braun/Betty is fully aware of the real world and functions as a virtual god within the simulation – he cannot be opposed or permanently harmed there, and he uses his omnipotence to enforce a cruel game on the player. Braun refuses to release James (who, it is revealed, has been transformed into a dog within the simulation as part of Braun’s cruel joke) until the player participates in a series of increasingly twisted tasks for Braun’s entertainment. What begins as relatively mischievous pranks – for example, breaking up a marriage or making a child cry – escalates into morally abhorrent acts, including murder. In the most extreme scenario, Braun directs the player to don the mask and knife of the fictional “Pint-Sized Slasher” and massacre all the other residents of Tranquility Lane, turning the cheerful neighborhood into a scene of horror. Throughout these events, Braun gleefully watches the suffering he orchestrates, then resets the simulation to start the cycle anew once he’s satisfied, trapping everyone in an endless loop of his making.
However, the Tranquility Lane simulation also contains a hidden alternative “failsafe” that the player can discover. This secret failsafe program, when activated, subverts Braun’s control: it triggers a scenario in which an army of virtual Chinese Communist soldiers invades Tranquility Lane and kills every resident almost instantly (a dark reference to the war that destroyed the outside world). In the real world, activating the failsafe causes the physical death of Vault 112’s remaining occupants in their pods, thus ending their suffering and permanently shutting down the simulation. Braun is left utterly alone, immortal but trapped in the now-empty virtual world he created – a fitting punishment for his atrocities. Regardless of how the player resolves the Tranquility Lane scenario (whether by obeying Braun’s sadistic tasks or by using the failsafe), the simulation ends and the Lone Wanderer is able to free James from his pod. Upon exiting Vault 112, James continues his mission to purify the Capital Wasteland’s water (resuming Project Purity), and the player’s main quest proceeds, while Dr. Braun remains behind, unable to escape the prison of his own making. Notably, Vault 112 does not reappear in subsequent Fallout games, making its Fallout 3 appearance a self-contained but memorable episode in the series.
## Reception and Legacy
Vault 112 and the Tranquility Lane quest are widely regarded as a standout segment of Fallout 3 for their unsettling atmosphere and inventive narrative design. Games journalists and players praised the quest’s blend of dark morality and retro Americana horror. In a retrospective on the series, PC Gamer described the Tranquility Lane sequence as “a Stepford Wives pastiche of affluent suburban living before the bombs fell” that is “inventive, dark, [and] humorous,” recapturing the weird, blackly comic tone of earlier Fallout entries. The cheerful vintage setting sharply contrasts with the grim cruelty of the player’s actions, exemplifying the franchise’s trademark dark humor and capacity for moral choice. Critic Jody Macgregor noted that Fallout 3’s overall tone grew significantly darker once the player stepped into Vault 112’s simulation – calling Tranquility Lane “Fallout 3 at its most twisted,” and observing that the quest “brings back” the series’ macabre sense of humor that had been missing up to that point. The scenario’s style and themes have also drawn comparisons to classic dystopian fiction; for example, its black-and-white, idyllic veneer concealing sadistic control is often likened to something out of The Twilight Zone or The Stepford Wives.
Aside from critical commentary, the developers of Fallout 3 themselves have highlighted Vault 112 as one of the game’s most notable creations. In a 2020 interview, lead designer Emil Pagliarulo and producer Jeff Gardiner revealed that Tranquility Lane is among their personal favorite quests in the Fallout series. Gardiner remarked that the Vault 112 sequence was “the perfect example” of the kind of darkly comedic, unexpected content the franchise allows, and noted that even years after release it still has a “wow” factor for players who experience it. Over a decade later, Vault 112’s Tranquility Lane continues to be remembered as one of the most disturbing and iconic moments in Fallout 3 – a segment that forcefully immerses the player in a moral dilemma within a hauntingly nostalgic simulation. Its legacy endures in discussions of the series’ best quests and serves as a prime example of the Fallout series’ unique blend of retro-futuristic whimsy and post-apocalyptic horror.

People will tell you the strangest and best parts of Bethesda RPGs are the sidequests, and sometimes that's true. (It certainly was in Oblivion.) But one of the most Wild Wasteland moments in Fallout 3 is part of the main storyline, sitting right there on the critical path.

WHY I LOVE

![Image 10: A wristwatch with Vault Boy on it](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/VHChYAZbi2P5kh8QByXMFh.jpg)

(Image credit: Bethesda)

In [Why I Love](https://www.pcgamer.com/uk/tag/why-i-love/), PC Gamer writers pick an aspect of PC gaming that they love and write about why it's brilliant. This week, Jody appreciates Fallout 3 at its most twisted.

Your quest in Fallout 3 is to find your dad, Liam Neeson. It's a better hook for an open world game than the search for your son in [Fallout 4](https://www.pcgamer.com/uk/fallout-4/), because everyone knows Liam Neeson can take care of himself. Bouncing across the Capital Wasteland, you're free to take your time—fight fire ants, help an inexplicably Canadian lady research her book—safe in the knowledge you can return to Dad Quest later on.

You finally track the deadbeat down to Vault 112, where you expect some kind of dungeon crawl, maybe a fight with some mutants or remnant Vault dwellers. You find something else entirely.

Vault 112's inhabitants have spent the last 200 years in a simulation, bodies suspended while their minds experience a series of pleasant virtual realities. Your dad went in to talk to the scientist who built it, Stanislaus Braun, and the only way to get him out is to follow. As the headset lowers over your face, the familiar loading screen message "PLEASE STAND BY" appears, to be replaced by the sedate black-and-white street called Tranquility Lane.

In this white picket fence American Dream, Fallout 3 becomes an episode of The Twilight Zone. While most of the residents are ignorant of their true nature, playing out their good neighbour roles in a place where there was no war and there is no wasteland, one is different. A little girl named Betty, watering flowers with her dog in the middle of this circular street, is aware of the real world. Her voice slips, becoming that of the elderly scientist Braun, and things get extremely Village of the Damned.

Braun's in charge of the simulation, a virtual god, and it's gone to his head. He's begun making the dream into a nightmare, tormenting the inhabitants for kicks then resetting reality, over and over, and will only hand over your dear old dad if you take part in his twisted game. You're a child too in the simulation, which makes it even more messed up when Braun's game escalates. The first task is making a boy cry; by the end you're committing atrocities.

![Image 11: A car parked in an all-American street](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/jVwaKPUioDweCnxPMoDSWN.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/jVwaKPUioDweCnxPMoDSWN.jpg)

I don't want to set the world on fire. Just this one street. (Image credit: Bethesda)

Fallout is at its best when it's offering multiple solutions to quests, letting you write your personality across its design. The first two games had three solutions for almost every problem—violent, diplomatic, or sneaky—but Fallout 3 often reduces that to two—good karma and bad karma. In Tranquility Lane, there are still good and bad karma options, but the bad karma ones branch like a network of arteries.

When Braun tells you to murder Mabel, it's suddenly a Hitman level in miniature, her house overflowing with deathtraps. You can sabotage a chandelier to fall on her, or go full Looney Tunes with a roller skate at the top of the stairs. You can talk to the neighbours to learn she loves to bake pies, then rig her gas oven to explode. Or you can hack her house's security to lock the doors and turn her Mr. Handy robot hostile, then evade the thing while it flamethrowers and saws her to death.

To top that, for a finale Braun tells you to become "the Pint-Sized Slasher." You find an evil clown mask and a knife, then kill every remaining adult in Tranquility Lane.

![Image 12: A child with a knife wearing a clown mask](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/2Zymr7cugk9HaQJW2NqAyT.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/2Zymr7cugk9HaQJW2NqAyT.jpg)

 A perfectly innocent normal child. With a knife. (Image credit: Bethesda)

Fallout is a black comedy from the moment you see US soldiers gunning down Canadians in the street during the first game's intro, but that dark sense of humor was lost in the sequel—replaced by sex jokes and pop culture references. Tranquility Lane brings it back. I can't help but laugh when I'm the Pint-Sized Slasher. The jaunty music, the bright surroundings, the clown mask, all absurdly contrasted with the simulated citizens who come apart at the joints just like the raiders you shoot for the other 50 hours you spend in Fallout 3.

"Wasn't it fun?" Braun asks afterwards. Sure it was. I was killing people in a videogame, that's what I signed up for. There's no way to spare them. The good karma choice is to activate a failsafe that kills the residents in real life, ending their torment while leaving Braun alone in this hell of his own making. Which is the darkest option yet. There's no way out of Tranquility Lane without blood on your hands.

![Image 9: Fallout 3](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/09b80c10631b1e922ab029c055c40d62.jpg)

'They've done it,' I thought, the moment I stumbled out of Vault 101 and the Capital wasteland came into focus. I traced the horizon with increasing excitement. Look at the blasted trees; and the little shattered towns; and the many, many shades of brown! The world reveal shot—when you emerge from a dark corridor to a carefully poised introductory vista—is familiar now, but in 2008 it set my spine shivering and filled my head with thoughts of freedom and adventure. The fact that I exercised that freedom to drink irradiated water from toilet cisterns the world over is neither here nor there—Fallout has always had a knack for being funny and grim at the same time.

The move to polygonal 3D and a generational leap in fidelity allowed Fallout 3 do more visual world-building and humour with sight-gags and signage. This and an all-knew writers' room shifted the style of Fallout's comedy from a quirky gangland farce to a quirky satire on the utopian idealism of the '50s and '60s, and a delightfully camp one at that. Robots stomp around powered by brains in jars and housekeeping robots are repurposed as death-bot bodyguards. Meanwhile, the comfy Jetsons family unit has been shattered and scattered across the wasteland. The family dogs have formed packs and started eating the adults. The kids live in their own settlement in Little Lamplight, and exiled teens rebel alone in Big Town.

![Image 10: Fallout 3 1](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/4b2b8b53b94be499568d1cbcb1b26462.jpg)

It's a bit depressing—as total societal collapse ought to be—but Fallout 3 strikes a fine balance between lonely wandering and silliness. Did you find the superhero and the supervillain warring in Cantebury Commons? The AntAgonizer leads an army of giant ants against the Mechanist's robot guards, and you can choose to side with either. Megaton's resident researcher, Moira, provides another memorable quest thread that sends you all over the wasteland to conduct field experiments. Irradiate yourself and she studies your symptoms with infectious enthusiasm—"keep up the great research, super assistant!"

Sadly Fallout 3's sidequests and secrets are more memorable than the critical path. A stone cold Liam Neeson continues Bethesda's dubious record with celebrity voice actors—unfortunate given that he's the emotional core of the story. There are some exceptional moments, however, like your entrapment in the Tranquility Lane simulation—a Stepford Wives pastiche of affluent suburban living before the bombs fell. It's inventive, dark, humourous, and recaptures a talent for weirdness that Bethesda hadn't exercised since Morrowind.

![Image 11: Fallout 3 3](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/fc9169df2b32159449f724dbfa949560.jpg)

It's violent, too, thanks to the real-time-with-pause combat system that lets you melt individual bodyparts with laser pistols. The "Bloody Mess" perk is recommended. The Gamebryo engine has many shortcomings—not least when it comes to NPC faces and posture—but it can chunk an enemy into slabs of physics-enabled mulch very nicely indeed. The VATS targeting system divides opinion, but the zooming Mad Max hero shots it generates for your wastelander are great. Such scenes were relegated to your imagination in the old turn-based RPGs, but now every shuddering headshot gets its own slow-mo rotating, zooming camera dance. If you're lucky, your Lone Wanderer will form an impromptu John Wayne silhouette against the green sky before you're popped back into real-time, where a lacklustre FPS-with-dice-rolls system awaits.

If that's not to your taste, Fallout 3's shortcomings can always be corrected with mods. Remove the green smog to enjoy a much cleaner, sunnier wasteland; or install major combat overhauls that ditch VATS in favour of a deadly survivalist shooter model inspired by STALKER. Fallout 3 features some pretty horrendous monsters—[Centaurs](http://fallout.wikia.com/wiki/Centaur_/(Fallout_3/)) still give me chills—but you can add even more terrors with Mart's Mutant Mod, and tweak their abilities and size to provide a challenge even when you're stomping around in full Brotherhood of Steel armour. Fallout 3 was great at release, but only got better in the following years, maturing to near-perfection like a fine pre-war vintage of Nuka Cola.

_By Tom Senior_
